\chapter{Di, Haz, Ve, Pon, Ten, Sal, Se, Ven}
\label{ch:command-irregular}
\hlchaptermodality{118}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the eight irregular informal commands and say why they are all one syllable.}

Complete ES-C50-ocho-cortos: give the eight forms and say why they are so short.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[di · haz · ve · pon · ten · sal · sé · ven]{di, haz, ve, pon, ten, sal, sé, ven}

\label{lesson:ES-C50-ocho-cortos}



\begin{quote}
By last chapter's rule, \textquotedblleft{}say it\textquotedblright{} should be \emph{dice}. It is not. There are exactly eight of these, and once you see them together you will not need to memorise the list.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: eight, all one syllable}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{command} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{decir} & \textbf{di} & say \\
\emph{hacer} & \textbf{haz} & do, make \\
\emph{ir} & \textbf{ve} & go \\
\emph{poner} & \textbf{pon} & put \\
\emph{tener} & \textbf{ten} & have, hold \\
\emph{salir} & \textbf{sal} & leave \\
\emph{ser} & \textbf{sé} & be \\
\emph{venir} & \textbf{ven} & come \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the middle column down. \textbf{Every single one is one syllable}, and most are two or three letters. No other set of forms in Spanish is this short.

That is the fact worth carrying, and it has a cause. A command is the sentence you shout, the sentence you say in a hurry, the sentence you interrupt somebody with. Words used that way get worn down harder than words used calmly — and these eight are the commonest verbs in the language, so they had the most use to be worn by.

So the list is not eight arbitrary exceptions. It is \textbf{what the eight most-shouted verbs look like after two thousand years of being shouted.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all eight in one breath — \textquotedblleft{}di, haz, ve, pon, ten, sal, sé, ven\textquotedblright{}
  \item each one as if calling across a room
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the list is a rhythm rather than eight facts.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many irregular \emph{tú} commands are there? (\textbf{Eight}.) What do they all have in common besides being irregular? (\textbf{One syllable each}.) Next: how to tell somebody \textbf{not} to do something — and you already have that form too.
\end{tcolorbox}
